A significant advancement over the previous generation of modified stagecoaches, the Mercedes 35 hp is regarded as the first modern car.

The bird-beaked vehicle had a 21.5-litre, 200 hp engine, and set a land speed record of 141 mph, said to be "faster than any plane, train, or automobile" at the time, a record that was not exceeded for ten years by any other vehicle.
The first true 'Bugatti', built in German Alsace before the region became part of France. The car pioneered multivalve engines and was a racing success.
Widely regarded as Britain’s first purpose-built sports car, designed for high-speed endurance trials.
Transformed global manufacturing with the introduction of the world’s first moving assembly line for mass automotive production. Over almost 20 years, Ford produced some 15 million models.
Earned the moniker "The Best Car in the World" during the 1910s via flawless reliability in gruelling trial events.
The Rumpler Tropfenwagen ("Rumpler drop car", named after its raindrop shape) was developed to be streamlined with a very low drag coefficient.
Britain's answer to the Ford Model T, an economic, mass-produced car, licensed and adapted across Europe, the US and Japan.
World’s first production car to feature a load-bearing monocoque chassis and independent front suspension.
A phenomenally successful racing car, winning over 1,000 races and pioneering the concept of a holistically conceived, race-ready car available for purchase
The first Chrysler car, technically advanced and an affordable price point.
Successfully replaced the Model T by introducing modern driver controls, standard safety glass, and contemporary styling.
Iconic endurance sports car that defined British racing pedigree.
Designed by Ferdinand Porsche, this supercharged performance car dominated hillclimbs and Grand Prix events worldwide.
The pinnacle of pre-war American luxury and power, featuring a DOHC 32-valve straight-eight engine capable of 116 mph.
The bespoke remodelling of the already luxury Cadillac V-16, ordered by by Philippe Barraud, a wealthy playboy of the 1930s, wanting an outrageous, bespoke automobile to suit his stylish lifestyle.
Dominant pre-war sports racer featuring a supercharged straight-eight engine and four consecutive Le Mans victories.
Pioneered mass-produced front-wheel drive combined with a steel monocoque chassis and independent suspension.
Early commercial attempt to introduce aerodynamic teardrop styling and cab-forward weight distribution to mass production.
World’s first production car equipped with an electrically powered retractable hardtop roof.
Groundbreaking American design featuring pop-up headlights, front-wheel drive, and a distinctive "coffin-nose" bonnet layout.
Pioneered the mid-engine layout for Grand Prix racing with a supercharged V16 engine designed by Ferdinand Porsche.
Compact, highly efficient packaging that democratised affordable mass motoring across Italy and broader Europe.
Apex of pre-war German luxury grand touring, featuring a supercharged straight-eight engine and bespoke coachwork.
Commissioned as an affordable rear-engined "people's car", laying the groundwork for one of the most produced vehicles in history.
Standardised light four-wheel-drive military vehicle that established the blueprint for all modern off-road vehicles.
Masterpiece of Pininfarina design that established the modern pontoon body shape with fully integrated wings and bonnet.
Advanced post-war safety pioneer featuring a central directional headlight, perimeter frame, and pop-out windscreen.
Introduced the legendary XK twin-cam engine and debuted as the fastest production car in the world.
Defined British civilian four-wheel-drive capability with its utilitarian aluminium bodywork and rugged chassis.
Alec Issigonis-designed family car that democratised post-war British motoring and became the first British vehicle to exceed one million sales.
The first production model to bear the Porsche name, establishing the brand's lightweight, rear-engine sports car identity.
Introduced aircraft-inspired tailfins and Cadillac's revolutionary high-compression overhead-valve V8 engine.
Pioneered "step-down" perimeter frame construction, creating an exceptionally low centre of gravity and sleek profile.
Paired a lightweight body with the high-compression Rocket V8 engine, establishing the blueprint for the American muscle car.
Aircraft-inspired front-wheel-drive compact car featuring an exceptionally low aerodynamic drag coefficient for its era.
Customised concept car that became television's first iconic superhero vehicle in the 1966 Batman series.
Established the archetype of the gadget-laden cinema "spy car" through its debut in Goldfinger.
Transformed a utilitarian mass-market vehicle into a beloved, sentient film franchise star in The Love Bug.
Immortalised in pop culture via the iconic bank-heist getaway chase through Turin in The Italian Job.
Revolutionised Hollywood stunt filming and set the gold standard for cinematic car chases in Bullitt.
Became Hollywood's definitive anti-hero muscle car in Bullitt and a prime-time TV icon as the "General Lee" in The Dukes of Hazzard.
Defined 1970s television cop culture with its distinctive "striped tomato" paint scheme in Starsky & Hutch.
Famous for its film transformation into a fully functional submarine in The Spy Who Loved Me.
Dominator of screen transport, starring in Smokey and the Bandit (1977) and as the AI-driven KITT in Knight Rider (1982).
Converted end-loading ambulance/hearse modified into the gadget-laden, siren-wailing transport for Ghostbusters.
Elevated an obscure, commercially failed sports car into an enduring global pop-culture legend via Back to the Future.
Immortalised as the ultimate symbol of automotive desire and teenage rebellion in Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.

Dominant Grand Prix car that secured victory in the inaugural Formula 1 World Championship race and back-to-back world titles.
Alfa Romeo’s first left-hand-drive car and first unitary chassis, marking the company's transition to mass assembly line manufacturing.
Lightweight compact sports car family that democratised race-derived twin-cam engine performance for mass motoring.

Lightweight, aluminium-panelled homologation special that achieved dominant success in touring car racing worldwide.
Iconic Pininfarina-designed roadster that remained in production across four distinct generations over nearly three decades.
Ultra-exclusive road-going derivative of the Tipo 33 racer featuring butterfly doors and an ultra-high-revving mid-mounted V8.
Groundbreaking front-wheel-drive compact hatchback praised for its boxer engine layout and exceptional dynamic handling.
Avant-garde Zagato-styled sports coupe engineered with race-derived suspension capable of extreme cornering forces.
European Car of the Year winner that revitalised the brand and introduced common-rail direct-injection diesel engines to production cars.
Benchmark high-performance sports saloon featuring a Ferrari-developed twin-turbo V6 engine and advanced active aerodynamics.
Agile rear-engined sports car that won the inaugural World Rally Championship for Manufacturers in 1973.
Revolutionised motorsport by introducing permanent all-wheel drive and turbocharged power to rallying.
Giant-killing lightweight saloon that famously won the Monte Carlo Rally three times in the 1960s.
Key machinery behind Citroën's era of total WRC dominance, securing the first seven of Sébastien Loeb's driver titles.
Unconventional entry featuring a front-overhang engine layout and hydropneumatic suspension that proved notoriously uncompetitive.
Three-time WRC Manufacturers' Champion that proved a family saloon could be turned into a rally giant-killer.
The definitive rear-wheel-drive gravel car of the 1970s, securing multiple driver and manufacturer world titles.
Purpose-built mid-engined spaceframe special created exclusively to maximize Group B technical regulations.
The world's first purpose-built rally supercar, winning three consecutive WRC manufacturers' titles.
The last rear-wheel-drive car to defeat four-wheel-drive competitors and win the WRC Manufacturers' Championship.
Group A icon that achieved an unprecedented six consecutive WRC Manufacturers' Championships.
Pioneered twincharging by integrating both a supercharger and a turbocharger to deliver instantaneous power.
Eschewed turbocharging in favour of a bespoke, naturally aspirated 3.0-litre V6 engine mated to four-wheel drive.
Highly developed Group A special that carried Tommi Mäkinen to four consecutive Drivers' Championships.
Simple and robust rear-wheel-drive machine that offered privateers high reliability in tough terrain.
Lightweight rear-wheel-drive contender utilizing extensive Kevlar bodywork to maintain high competitive speed.
Mid-engined, all-wheel-drive Group B masterpiece that claimed back-to-back WRC titles in 1985 and 1986.
Advanced technological platform featuring computer-controlled four-wheel drive developed for Group B homologation.
The ultimate tarmac-focused iteration of the mid-engined 5 Turbo, extracting massive power from a 1.5-litre engine.
Iconic all-wheel-drive performer that defined 1990s WRC culture and propelled Colin McRae to his 1995 world title.
Modern benchmark for hybrid-era WRC technology, continuing Toyota's long lineage of championship success.
Earned the nickname "King of Africa" by dominating brutal endurance events like the Safari Rally through sheer durability.
Defined the 1.6-litre turbo era by winning four consecutive driver and manufacturer championship doubles.
Dominated the inaugural World Championship season, winning every Grand Prix it entered in 1950.
Iconic front-engined racer driven to legendary victories by Juan Manuel Fangio and Stirling Moss.
Introduced desmodromic valves, direct fuel injection, and streamlined bodywork options to Formula 1.
The first mid-engined car to win the Formula 1 World Championship, triggering an engine-placement revolution.
Revolutionised F1 chassis design by introducing the fully integrated monocoque structure.
Pioneered using the engine (Ford Cosworth DFV) as a fully stressed structural chassis member.
Introduced side-mounted radiators, inboard front brakes, and wedge aerodynamics that shaped the modern F1 silhouette.
The definitive ground-effect F1 car that exploited underbody Venturi tunnels for unprecedented cornering speeds.
Pioneered the use of a lightweight, ultra-rigid carbon-fibre composite monocoque chassis.
The first turbocharged car to win the Formula 1 Drivers' World Championship.
One of the most dominant cars in F1 history, claiming victory in 15 out of 16 races during the 1988 season.
Technologically supreme machine equipped with active suspension, traction control, and semi-automatic transmission.
The apex of the V10 era that set longstanding lap records during Michael Schumacher's seventh title season.
Fairytale championship winner famous for its game-changing double diffuser aerodynamic innovation.
Benchmark of the early turbo-hybrid era, securing 19 victories and 20 pole positions out of 21 races.
Statistically the most dominant F1 car ever built, winning 21 out of 22 Grand Prix races in a single season.
